title: Die with Zero: Getting All You Can from Your Money and Your Life
author: Bill Perkins
review:
Good introduction to this concept but a little bit shallow with a lot of anecdotes that aren't generally applicable as well as pretty light (almost non existent) material for how to implement this strategy.

This is probably only good for a certain type of person whose inclination is to hoard wealth and not actually use it in meaningful ways that measurably improve the quality of life at the time where it's most needed.

I do think the sections talking about when most people receive inheritance and how much of an impact they have are interesting and important as well as thinking critically on phases of life and when to use the resources you have instead of waiting until health declines and you can no longer effectively enjoy the fruits of your labor.

As always though there's a massive amount of uncertainty especially when the time horizon is so long and no one has a simple or clear answer for how to actually have the perfect amount of savings for retirement. I think this is worth reading parts of this if you get it from the library like I did and treat it as sort of an extended blog post.

highlights.text: So buying an experience doesn’t just buy you the experience itself—it also buys you the sum of all the dividends that experience will bring for the rest of your life.
No, the key takeaway, I now realize, is to strike the right balance between spending on the present (and only on what you value) and saving smartly for the future.
Being aware that your time is limited can clearly motivate you to make the most of the time you do have.
survival threshold = 0.7 × (cost to live one year) × (years left to live)
